kurz: How the Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Calmar ratio and information ratio are constructed, what they fail to capture and how easily they can be dressed up.

bloecke.md:
A return figure on its own is not enough to judge an investment. A return of 9% a year can come from a portfolio that was never more than 15% down along the way, or from a portfolio that at times had lost two-thirds of its value. Risk metrics are meant to make this difference measurable.

Almost all of them divide the **excess return**, that is, the return minus a threshold, by a measure of risk. They differ in two choices. The first is the threshold above which a return counts. This can be zero, the risk-free rate or the return of a benchmark index. The second is the risk measure in the denominator. The candidates are fluctuation in both directions, fluctuation on the downside only, market sensitivity or the deepest decline suffered. With these two pieces of information, a metric can be read correctly, and you can tell when it has been conveniently tailored.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula measures the return above the risk-free rate per unit of fluctuation. Values from shorter periods are scaled up to a year with the square root of the number of periods (annualised), so a monthly Sharpe ratio is multiplied by sqrt(12).
variablen: risk-free rate for the same period
bloecke.beispiel: MSCI World (net, euros) 2001-2025: 6.26% p.a. geometric, standard deviation of annual returns 17.71%, assumed risk-free rate 2.0% → (6.26 − 2.00) / 17.71 = 0.24.

bloecke.md: The Sharpe ratio has three peculiarities. First, it treats upward swings in the same way as downward swings. A year with a gain of 45% therefore also increases the standard deviation in the denominator, and the Sharpe ratio rises less than the higher return alone would make it rise. Second, it assumes that annualisation with the square root is permissible, which only holds for uncorrelated periods. Third, it becomes useless as soon as the excess return is negative. With an excess return of minus four percentage points, a volatility of 10% gives a value of −0.40, whereas a volatility of 20% gives −0.20. The riskier portfolio then comes out better. Broadly diversified equity indices are usually below 1 over long periods. If a sustained Sharpe ratio above 2 is reported, the first question to ask is about the time window.

Target return freely selectable, few data points in the denominator
ignores unsystematic risk, only meaningful for components of a broad portfolio
Benchmark freely selectable, reliable verdict only after decades
rarely used, not found in factsheets

bloecke.md: The Sortino ratio replaces the standard deviation with the **downside deviation**. Only periods below a self-chosen target return are included, as squared deviations, and everything above counts as zero. This comes closer to what investors perceive as risk. At the same time, this is its weak point, because the target return is not prescribed. The Calmar ratio relates the return to the deepest decline. Terry Young defined it in 1991 over 36 months. In practice, it is often calculated over the entire available period, which makes the values incomparable. The least known is Peter Martin's Ulcer index. Among the drawdown measures, which measure declines from the peak, it is the most informative.

bloecke.formel: Ulcer index = sqrt( (R1² + R2² + … + RN²) / N ),  Ri = 100 × (Price_i − previous peak) / previous peak
bloecke.erklaerung: Each point in time enters with the square of its distance from the previous peak. A deep decline weighs more than a shallow one, a long one more than a short one. The maximum drawdown captures only the lowest point, while the Ulcer index also captures how long the investment stayed below its peak.
bloecke.beispiel: Martin ratio = (Return − risk-free rate) / Ulcer index.

## Four equity markets compared by metric

The following table works through four equity markets over the same period. It is based on calendar-year returns from 2001 to 2025 in euros. The return is calculated as a geometric mean, and the risk-free rate is assumed to be a constant 2.0%. The downside deviation refers to this target. Drawdown and Ulcer index are based on year-end values, and beta is measured against the MSCI World.

bloecke.titel: Nine metrics for four equity markets, 2001-2025 (euros)
zeilen: Treynor (percentage points per unit of beta)

bloecke.titel: Rankings by four metrics over 25 years
bloecke.unter: By the Sharpe ratio, the world index and emerging markets are level; by the Sortino and Martin ratios, emerging markets lead clearly. The DAX has the lowest value on all four metrics.

bloecke.md: The change in the ranking has an understandable cause. At 24.4%, emerging markets fluctuated considerably more than developed markets, but a large part of this fluctuation came from price rises. In 2009, for example, the index gained 72.9% in euros. The Sharpe ratio counts such rises as risk, the Sortino ratio does not. In addition, after the 2008 crash the emerging markets index was back at its old peak by the end of 2010. The MSCI World in euros took until the end of 2013 to get there and thus spent twelve calendar years below its old high. The Ulcer index captures this duration, which is why the ranking changes with it.

bloecke.titel: MSCI World in euros, twelve years below its peak
bloecke.unter: On a year-end basis (end of 2000 = 100), the index was below its starting level from 2001 to 2012. On this basis, the lowest point is −41.6%, on a daily basis −53.6%.

bloecke.md:
The most important property of the maximum drawdown is its dependence on how it is measured. The value therefore does not describe the investment alone. Year-end data for the MSCI World in euros give −41.6%, daily data for the period from 24 May 2001 to 9 March 2009 give −53.6%. The finer the data frequency and the longer the history, the deeper the reported decline. Comparing two funds by their maximum drawdown therefore only makes sense with the same frequency and the same period. Otherwise you are comparing measurement methods instead of funds.

A fixed arithmetic rule applies to the recovery after a decline. After a loss of 20%, a gain of 25% is needed to get back to the starting level, after a loss of 50% a gain of 100%, and after a loss of 80% a gain of 400%.

bloecke.titel: Rolling ten-year Sharpe ratio, annual data in euros
bloecke.unter: With the same investment, formula and currency and the same assumed interest rate of 2%, the Sharpe ratio ranges between −0.27 and +1.11, depending on the period.

bloecke.md: The MSCI World had a Sharpe ratio of −0.27 in the decade to 2009 and one of 1.11 in the decade to 2021. In addition, the lines cross several times. In the windows ending in 2006 to 2015, the DAX came out ahead, and after that it was consistently behind. Every metric in a prospectus therefore describes first the chosen period and only then the investment. If a time window has an unusual cut-off, such as three and a half years, since launch or since a change of strategy, the starting point has usually been chosen deliberately.

## Tracking error and information ratio

The **tracking error** is the standard deviation of the return difference between a portfolio and its benchmark index. It measures the width of the deviations and says nothing about costs or shortfall. It should be distinguished from the tracking difference, which for ETFs denotes the realised return gap to the index. The **information ratio** relates the average active return, that is, the return difference to the benchmark index, to the tracking error. It indicates the return per unit of deliberately accepted deviation.

One example is a German portfolio that holds only the DAX instead of the world index. Against the MSCI World in euros, its tracking error from 2001 to 2025 was 11.6 percentage points, with an average active return of 0.09 percentage points. This gives an information ratio of 0.01. Over a quarter of a century, this portfolio took on a considerable deviation without receiving any additional return for it. An MSCI ACWI has a tracking error of 1.8 percentage points against the MSCI World. Here, the same metric describes a completely different degree of deviation.

The t-statistic shows how clearly an information ratio stands out from chance. It is approximately `t = IR × sqrt(years)`. An information ratio of around 0.5 is considered good and corresponds to a manager in the top quartile. To reach the usual significance threshold of 1.96 with it, you need (1.96 / 0.5)² ≈ 15.4 years of clean data. With an information ratio of 0.25, it is already around 61 years.

For comparison, the DAX beat the world index from 2001 to 2012 with an information ratio of 0.26 (t = 0.26 × sqrt(12) = 0.90). From 2016 to 2025 it lagged behind at −0.28 (t = −0.89). Neither value is statistically significant. In an advertising brochure of their time, both would nevertheless have looked convincing.

bloecke.titel: Sharpe ratio under five permissible conventions
bloecke.unter: Sharpe ratio of the MSCI World (net, EUR) 2001-2025. There is a factor of 2.5 between the highest and the lowest figure, and all figures are correctly calculated.

bloecke.titel: Ways to dress up the numbers
bloecke.md:
- The choice of time window has the strongest effect, as shown above.
- If the risk-free rate is set at zero instead of 3%, the Sharpe ratio almost doubles.
- Using the arithmetic instead of the geometric mean raises the return by approximately σ²/2, at 18% volatility by around 1.6 percentage points a year.
- Monthly instead of daily data smooth the path and make drawdowns appear smaller.
- Valuations can be smoothed if prices are estimated rather than traded. Measured volatility then falls and the Sharpe ratio rises, without any change in the risk.
- By switching the benchmark index, an information ratio can be generated almost at will.
- The metric itself can also be swapped, for example Sortino instead of Sharpe or Calmar instead of Sortino, depending on which turns out more favourable.
- Calculations are done gross instead of net, for example with index returns that include neither fund costs nor taxes.

bloecke.titel: Effect of tax on metrics (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.md:
The assumptions are an equity fund that delivers the 6.26% p.a. of the MSCI World and an instant-access savings account paying 2.00%. Further assumptions are taxation only at the end and losses that can be fully offset. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) and the deferral effect of the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) are disregarded.

For equity funds, a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% applies, and the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) including solidarity surcharge is 26.375%. The effective burden is therefore 26.375% × 70% = 18.46%, and 6.26% × 0.8154 = 5.10% of the fund's return remains. There is no partial exemption for the savings account, so 2.00% × 0.73625 = 1.47% remains here.

The excess return thus falls from 4.26 to 3.63 percentage points, that is, by just under 15%. If the fluctuation is reduced in the same proportion as the fund's return (factor 0.8154), the result is a Sharpe ratio of 3.63 / 14.44 = 0.25. This is practically the same value as before tax (0.24). The ratio therefore stays almost the same, although one-seventh of the risk premium disappears. Costs and taxes partly cancel out in the metric, but not in your wealth.

Before you trust a metric, these points should be clarified:

1. The period, and the reason for this start and this end.
2. The data frequency (daily, monthly or annual).
3. The risk-free rate, the target return and the benchmark index.
4. The type of mean (arithmetic or geometric).
5. Whether costs and taxes are taken into account.
6. How the same investment looks on a second metric with a different denominator.

For fund selection, metrics are suitable for screening out, but not for picking. They reliably show how an investment has behaved. As a forecast they are weak, because their variation from period to period is greater than the difference between the products being compared.

As a fraction, each of these metrics expresses a particular view of what risk is. The denominator determines the ranking, the time window the level. A metric without details of period, frequency, reference rate and benchmark index is therefore not meaningful.

Annualising a monthly Sharpe ratio with sqrt(12) assumes that successive monthly returns are uncorrelated. For liquid equity indices this is a usable approximation, for other investments it is not. If returns are positively autocorrelated, meaning that good months tend to be followed by good ones and bad months by bad ones, the true annual volatility grows faster than the square root. The annualised Sharpe ratio is then too high. Positive autocorrelation is typical of investments with estimated rather than traded prices. With negatively autocorrelated returns, by contrast, the annualised Sharpe ratio is too low.

Sharpe ratios of different asset classes are therefore only comparable if they come from the same data frequency. Comparing a metric calculated from monthly data with one calculated from quarterly data is a calculation error.

mitnehmen: Almost all common risk metrics divide an excess return by a measure of risk and differ only in what counts as the threshold and what counts as risk.
The denominator changes the ranking of two investments; emerging markets, for example, are behind the world index by Sharpe and clearly ahead of it by Sortino and Martin.
The maximum drawdown depends on how it is measured; for the MSCI World in euros, annual data show −41.6% and daily data −53.6%.

For a fixed period, the risk-free rate and the choice of mean change the same Sharpe ratio by a factor of 2.5, and depending on the time window it ranges between −0.27 and 1.11 for the MSCI World, without any of the figures being wrong.
With an information ratio of 0.5, you need around fifteen years of data to distinguish the result statistically from chance.

begriffe.text: The return above the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of returns. It measures the return per unit of total fluctuation and treats upward swings in the same way as downward swings.
A standard deviation that only takes into account periods below a specified target return. It forms the denominator of the Sortino ratio.
The largest percentage decline from the previous peak to the subsequent trough. Its value depends heavily on data frequency and measurement period.
The square root of the mean of the squared distances from the previous peak. It captures the depth and duration of declines and is the basis of the Martin ratio.
The standard deviation of the return difference between a portfolio and its benchmark index. It measures the width of the deviations, not the shortfall.
The average active return against a benchmark index divided by the tracking error. It indicates the return per unit of deliberately accepted deviation.
